schools.summary: Gill explains Ramathaim as a dual, two Ramahs, the city consisting of two parts built perhaps on two hills, and offers several accounts of Zophim: that the Rabbins take the hills to have looked one at another; that being on eminences they had watchtowers with watchmen set in them; that the word means prophets, who are sometimes called watchmen, so that a school of the prophets stood here, a reading the Targum seems to countenance when it renders the clause there was one man of Ramatha, of the disciples of the prophets; or that the man was simply one of the Ramathites and of the family of Zuph, which gave its name to the land of Zuph. He records from Jerome that this is the Arimathaea of Joseph, in the Thamnitic region near Lydda.

Henry takes Elkanah for a Levite of the family of the Kohathites, the most honourable house of that tribe, whose ancestor Zuph was an Ephrathite, that is of Bethlehem-Judah which was called Ephrathah; there this family of the Levites was first seated, and one branch of it afterwards removed to Mount Ephraim, from which Elkanah descended. He suggests that notice is taken of their being originally Ephrathites in order to show their alliance to David. On the school of the prophets he is decidedly negative: prophecy, he thinks, revived in Samuel, since before his time there was for a great while no open vision, and scarcely a prophet of the Lord is mentioned from Moses to Samuel, so that we have no reason to think there was any nursery or college of prophets at Ramah until Samuel himself founded one there.

Clarke treats the verse as the opening of a book and states the older arrangement, that these were formerly reckoned the four books of Kings and that the two books of Samuel anciently made but one, the separation seeming to him to have been done without reason or necessity; properly speaking, he holds, they are a continuation of the book of Judges. On the authorship he reports rather than endorses: because most Hebrew copies bear Samuel's name as a running title he has generally been supposed the author, though the name does not appear to have been anciently prefixed, and the Jews commonly hold that he wrote the first twenty-seven chapters while Gad and Nathan added the last four, an opinion founded on the verse in Chronicles that names the books of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer. Wesley notes only that the place is called Ramah in the nineteenth verse, and that Elkanah was of Bethlehem-Judah by birth and habitation though by his original a Levite.

Ellicott runs through the derivations of Zophim and then chooses: the reference to the prophet-watchmen of the house of Israel is interesting though fanciful, and the simplest and least strained explanation refers the name to the hills so placed that they watched one another, or better still to watch-towers built at an early date on the two summits. He takes Ephrathite here to mean Ephraimite, explaining it by civil standing rather than by descent — Elkanah was a Levite of the family of Kohath who belonged, so far as his civil standing was concerned, to the tribe among whom he lived — and he answers the difficulty some have found in reconciling Samuel's Levitical descent with his mother's dedication of him, since Levitical service began only at twenty-five and even then was not continuous, whereas Samuel's dedication was life-long. On the opening formula he denies what Clarke infers: the words do not signify that this history is the continuation of the Book of Judges or of any preceding writing, being a common historical introductory formula found at the head of Joshua, Ruth, Esther, Ezra and Ezekiel. Keil is concerned with the division rather than the join, noting that the books originally formed one undivided work and in the Hebrew manuscripts do so still, the split into two having originated with the Alexandrian translators and reached the printed Hebrew Bible only in the sixteenth century; the Greek title books of the kingdoms he allows so far as each of the two works contains the history of a double kingdom, here the kingdoms of Saul and David.

debates.question: Was there already a school of the prophets at Ramah?

positions.position: the name Zophim, watchers, and the Targum's disciples of the prophets suggest one stood there
no; prophecy revived in Samuel, and no nursery of prophets existed at Ramah until he founded one
the prophet-watchmen derivation is interesting but fanciful; the name comes from the two hills or their watch-towers
of Bethlehem-Judah, which was called Ephrathah, where the family was first seated
Ephraimite — a Levite by descent who belonged for civil purposes to the tribe among whom he lived

debates.question: Does the opening word make this book a continuation of Judges?

positions.position: yes; properly speaking these books continue Judges, and their separation from one another was done without reason
no; it is a common historical introductory formula, standing at the head of several unconnected books

outliers.note: attends to the division rather than the opening, tracing the split into two books to the Alexandrian translators and its entry into the printed Hebrew Bible to the sixteenth century

a Levite called an Ephrathite
whether the book continues Judges

2.pericope_label: Two wives, the yearly sacrifice, and Peninnah's provocation

schools.summary: Gill says the two wives were connived at in those times but contrary to the original law of marriage, and that Elkanah, though a good man, was chastised for it with a great deal of vexation and trouble, his wives never agreeing; he guesses that Peninnah was taken because Hannah bore no children. Of the yearly going up he takes the phrase from solemn feast to solemn feast, there being three in the year at which every male was to appear, and notes that a Levite would be the more careful to observe the rule. On the portion given to Hannah he reports the Targum's one choice portion, the best part of the peace offering after the priest's share, and observes that the word is dual, so that some render it a double portion and others one part of two faces. Of the provocation he says that where a man had more wives than one they were usually at enmity, each jealous lest the other have more of the husband's love, and that Peninnah upbraided Hannah with her barrenness continually.

Clarke states the rule from experience, that wherever there was more than one wife we find the peace of the family greatly disturbed, and gives the meanings of the two names, Hannah fixed or settled and Peninnah a jewel or pearl. He observes that this is the first place in the Bible where the Lord of hosts occurs, takes the hosts for the heavenly bodies, and argues that to call Jehovah their Lord was to declare him their Maker and Governor and therefore the proper object of religious worship rather than they — at once showing the superiority of Israel's religion to all that heathenism could boast. Of the difficult phrase for Hannah's portion he says the Hebrew is very obscure and lays the versions side by side, the Syriac giving double, the Chaldee chosen, the Vulgate that he being sorrowful gave her one part. He turns Elkanah's closing question into its own answer: is not his especial affection better than all the comfort a numerous family could give? Wesley agrees that the second marriage was a transgression of the original institution of marriage and probably occasioned by Hannah's barrenness; he notes that as a Levite Elkanah went up at other times besides the three feasts, in his course, and that Peninnah was the more exasperated at the feasts because there the family were thrown together on the road and in their lodgings, whereas at home they had distinct apartments.

Ellicott sets the polygamy in a longer frame, observing that the primeval divine ordination sanctioned monogamy alone, and that in the Mosaic code polygamy is accepted as a custom everywhere prevailing but never approved, the laws seeking, as with slavery, only to restrict and limit it; the writer here, he thinks, quietly shows up the curse which almost invariably attended this violation of the home, one of the many gently-worded but fire-tipped rebukes the Old Testament directs at sins condoned and even approved by the voice of mankind. On the yearly journey he narrows the reference, since the Hebrew word rendered yearly is the one used of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, so that there is little doubt the Passover is meant. He counts the title Lord of hosts some two hundred and sixty times in the Old Testament, finds it in none of the books compiled before this one, and thinks it significant that it should first appear in the books which tell of the setting up of an earthly throne, as the protest of Samuel and his school against any eclipsing of the invisible sovereignty by the passing splendours of a monarchy. With Keil he reads Hannah's portion as one portion for two persons, a double share given as a sign, in Von Gerlach's words, that thou art as dear to me as if thou hadst borne me a child; he grants that the Vulgate, Luther and Abarbanel favour the reading which turns the husband unkind, but holds the double portion preferable both grammatically and exegetically. Of the provocation he says the one sin poisons a household otherwise quiet and Godfearing, Peninnah choosing the solemn occasion of the thank-offering to refer her rival's childlessness to the special anger of God. Keil adds only that ten is a round number for many.

debates.question: What was the worthy portion given to Hannah?

positions.position: a double portion, one portion for two persons, given as a sign of his love
the best single portion left after the priest's share, the dual form leaving the reading open
the Hebrew is very obscure, the versions dividing between double, chosen, and a portion given sorrowfully
the three solemn feasts at which every male was to appear, and for a Levite his course besides
the Passover, since the Hebrew phrase for yearly is the one used of the Feast of Unleavened Bread

outliers.note: reads the first appearance of Lord of hosts as deliberate, a protest lodged by Samuel and his school against the coming monarchy eclipsing the invisible King

themes: polygamy and the peace of the house
the first Lord of hosts in scripture
Hannah's portion at the sacrificial meal

9.pericope_label: Hannah rises from the meal; Eli on his seat

schools.summary: Gill reads the clause of the whole party, who had eaten heartily and drunk freely and made a feast of it where the tabernacle and altar were; but he notes that the Targum makes it after she had eaten and drunk, on the ground that her husband's entreaty may have prevailed on her to eat somewhat, though little, and to drink, though it were but water, since she afterwards declares she had touched neither wine nor strong drink.

Henry finds the gentle reproof already working: it brought her to her meat, for she did not harden herself in sorrow nor grow sullen when she was reproved, but perceiving her husband uneasy that she would not come and eat with them, she cheered up her own spirits as well as she could and came to table. It also brought her to her prayers, putting her upon considering — do I well to be angry, do I well to fret, what good does it do me? Had I not better ease myself of the burden and cast it upon the Lord by prayer? Her husband's question, whether he were not better to her than ten sons, may have started the thought that whether he be so or no, God is, and therefore to him will I apply and before him will I pour out my complaint. The moment, Henry adds, was as well chosen as the place: they were at the door of the tabernacle, where God had promised to meet his people; they had lately offered their peace-offerings and, taking the comfort of being accepted, had feasted upon the sacrifice; and now it was proper to put up her prayer in virtue of that sacrifice, since by a peace-offering not only is atonement made for sin but the audience and acceptance of our prayers is obtained. To that sacrifice, in all our supplications, we must have an eye.

Clarke takes the seat for the throne of judgment, since Eli was then judge of Israel, and thinks this the first place where the temple of Jehovah is named at all — which gives room for a strong suspicion that these books were not compiled until the first temple was built, or later still. Wesley grants the seat was manifestly raised higher than ordinary but holds that Eli sat there rather as high priest, to hear and answer such as came to him for advice and to inspect and direct the worship of God; the temple, he says in a line, means the tabernacle, which is frequently so called.

Ellicott calls the meal the solemn sacrificial one at which the whole family were present, and takes the seat as both throne and bench at once, a chair of state where the high-priestly judge sat at certain times to administer justice. He adds that Eli was of the line of Ithamar, the younger son of Aaron, though what moved the dignity across from the elder line of Eleazar is lost. On the word temple he takes a middle way between Clarke and Wesley: the Hebrew word rendered post, and the later mention of the doors of the house, seem to suggest that a permanent home had by now been raised for the sanctuary, something of a building, possibly of stone, surrounding the tabernacle; and he would render the phrase palace of the Lord, so called not from any external magnificence but as the earthly place where at times the visible glory of Israel's King was pleased to manifest itself. Keil marks the rising as the turn of the story, Hannah getting up with a troubled heart when the sacrificial meal was over to pour out her grief in prayer before God.

debates.question: In what capacity was Eli sitting by the post?

positions.position: as judge, upon the throne of judgment, being then judge of Israel
rather as high priest, to answer those who came for advice and to direct the worship of God
as both, on a chair of state where the high-priestly judge sat at times to administer justice

debates.question: What does the phrase temple of the Lord imply about the sanctuary?

positions.position: that the books were not compiled until the first temple was built, or later still
nothing; the word simply means the tabernacle, which is frequently so called
that a permanent building, possibly of stone, had by now been raised around the tabernacle; the word is better rendered palace, from the glory that dwelt there rather than from magnificence

outliers.note: reads the verse as the fruit of the husband's reproof, tracing the movement from the table to the prayer and grounding the prayer itself in the peace-offering they had just eaten

themes: the meal and the rising
whether Eli sat as judge or as priest
what the word temple implies here

10.pericope_label: The vow, the silent prayer, and Eli's mistake

schools.summary: Gill raises the legal question the others pass by: a woman's vow was void if her husband disapproved, and Jewish tradition holds that a man may vow his son a Nazarite but a woman may not — a tradition this verse contradicts, which is why, he says, they labour to explain the vow away. Of the manner of her praying he takes the phrase to mean she was earnest and importunate, repeating her petition and prolonging her prayer, unwilling to let the Lord go until she had some satisfaction that she should have what she asked, some thinking she continued an hour; and he calls it mental prayer, ejaculations of her mind which she knew were well known to God without being expressed vocally. Of the rebuke he supposes a longer history behind it, since the words sound like what, every day drunk, continually in this wicked practice, so that Eli may have observed odd looks and a strange behaviour in her at other times which he had put down to wine; the Targum has him ask instead how long she will behave like a fool or a mad woman.

Clarke marks how much the vow added to what was owed already: as a descendant of Levi the boy was the Lord's property from twenty-five years of age to fifty, but this pledged him from infancy to death and made him not a Levite only but a Nazarite, on whose head no razor should pass. He says of the silent prayer that her whole heart was engaged, and that though she spake not with an audible voice her lips formed themselves according to the pronunciation of the words her heart uttered. Wesley says the vow in six words, a perpetual Nazarite, and reads the Hebrew of her long praying as multiplied to pray, drawing a rule from it: she plainly said much more than is here expressed, and the like is to be judged of the prayers and sermons of other holy persons in scripture, which give us only the sum and substance of them. He points at the scene itself for the cause of Eli's suspicion — the multitude of her words and those motions of her face and body which the vehemency of her passion and her fervency in prayer occasioned.

Ellicott counts two promises in the vow: the first pledged the son to the service of the Eternal all the days of his life, though the mother looked only to a life-long service in the ritual of the Tabernacle and God destined him for higher work, the priestly duties soon merging in the far more responsible ones of the prophet and reformer of the people; the second undertook that he should be a Nazarite, which included refraining from intoxicating drink, letting the hair grow, and avoiding all ceremonial defilement by corpses even of the nearest kin. Samuel, he notes, was what the Talmud calls a perpetual Nazarite, and the untouched hair singled out here was a public protest that he had renounced intercourse with the world and devoted the whole fulness of life to the Lord's work. Following Bunsen, he turns the charge of drunkenness back on the sanctuary: Eli was struck with dismay at her silent earnestness, such heartfelt prayer being apparently not usual at that time, and remembering the state of the moral life in the precincts over which he ruled with so weak and vacillating a rule, and how sadly frequent disorders were at the sacrificial meal, he at once suspected that the weeping woman was drunk — though he quickly atoned for the unworthy suspicion. Keil keeps to what the verse says, that Eli noticed her mouth, saw the lips move without a voice, and told her to put away her wine, that is, to go away and sleep off her intoxication; the idiom for her praying he renders speaking to her heart.

debates.question: Why did Eli take Hannah for a drunken woman?

positions.position: he had probably seen odd looks and strange behaviour in her at other times and put them down to wine
the multitude of her words and the motions of her face and body, which her vehemence in prayer occasioned
her silent earnestness was unusual for that day, and disorders at the sacrificial meal were sadly frequent in the precincts he ruled so weakly

outliers.note: notices that Jewish law made a wife's vow void without her husband's consent and that tradition denied a woman the right to vow her son a Nazarite — a rule this verse contradicts, and which the tradition therefore labours to explain away

themes: the two promises of the vow
praying in the heart
why Eli thought her drunk

schools.summary: Gill takes her opening words as spoken with great mildness and meekness, without falling into a passion at so scandalous an imputation, and with the respect due to Eli's office; but he also records the other tradition, which hears an edge in them — that he was no lord in this matter, and that the Holy Ghost did not rest upon him, which he had sufficiently shown by suspecting her at all. He takes daughter of Belial in the ordinary sense of a yokeless, lawless, impudent and abandoned creature, one of the vilest of wretches, as she must be who came drunk into the sanctuary of God, adding that drunkenness is an abominable crime in a man but much more in a woman, the Romans having made it in them a capital offence. Of Eli's change of mind he notes what caused it, that her discourse was not only sober and rational but religious and spiritual, so that he dismissed her in peace and bade her not distress herself with what he had said.

Clarke admires the construction of her vindication — neither wine nor inebriating drink has been poured out unto me, but I have poured out my soul unto the Lord — which he calls a great deal of delicacy and point. He construes the next phrase differently from the others, as put not thy handmaid before the faces of a daughter of Belial, that is, expose me not to reproach before such women, several of whom probably attended at the sanctuary for the purposes of prostitution and gain, since we read soon after that the sons of Eli lay with the women at the door of the tabernacle; and he draws the conclusion from both halves of the scene, that the high priest could suppose a praying woman drunk and that such women were to be found there at all, proving religion was at a very low ebb in Shiloh.

Ellicott quotes Calvin for the meek reading of her answer, that we should consider the modesty of Hannah, who though she had received injury from the high priest yet answers with reverence and humility, and sets beside it the Talmudic tradition that she meant the opposite. He makes Eli's reply a window on the whole character: weak and over-indulgent to his headstrong wicked sons, probably too self-indulgent and a lover of ease, Eli yet shows flashes of true nobility, real generosity and self-forgetfulness which light up a life that closed in failure and disaster, and here he is quick to see that he has been insulting a blameless woman, retracts the cruel accusation at once, accuses himself of precipitancy in his courteous farewell, and in his fatherly wish almost promises her what she had asked. Of her going away he offers the Speaker's Commentary's judgment, that it is a beautiful example of the composing influence of prayer, since she had cast her burden upon the Lord and so her own spirit was relieved of its load, and she returned to the feast and ate her portion with a cheerful heart. Keil insists that Eli's word was not a prediction but a pious wish, which God in his grace most gloriously fulfilled, and says she was strengthened and comforted by it as assuring her that her prayer would be heard, the text leaving the reader to supply the missing word — her countenance was no more troubled, as it had been. Wesley traces the change further back, to God's Spirit setting the priest's words home upon her and assuring her that both his prayers and hers should be heard.

debates.question: How is Hannah's answer to be heard?

positions.position: with meekness and reverence, as one who had received injury from the high priest and yet answered humbly
on the Talmudic reading, as a rebuke — thou art no lord in this matter, nor does the Holy Spirit rest upon thee

debates.question: What does she ask Eli not to do?

positions.position: not to count her one of the daughters of Belial, lawless creatures such as a woman must be who came drunk into the sanctuary
not to expose her to reproach before such women, several of whom probably attended the sanctuary for prostitution and gain

outliers.note: guards Eli's word from being read as prophecy, calling it a pious wish which God in his grace most gloriously fulfilled

a daughter of Belial

19.pericope_label: They worship and return; the Lord remembers Hannah

schools.summary: Gill gives the plain reason for the early rising, partly devotion and partly the journey before them.

Henry will not let the detail go so quickly. Observe, he says, how they improved their time at the tabernacle: every day they were there, even the day fixed for going home, they worshipped God, and rose early to do it — it is good to begin the day with God, and let him that is the first have the first. They had a journey before them and a family of children to take with them, and yet they would not stir till they had worshipped God together, for prayer and provender do not hinder a journey; they had already spent several days in religious worship and yet attended once more, since we should not be weary of well-doing. Of the remembering he says it was the answer to the exact thing she had asked, the very thing she desired and more she needed not desire, and draws the general comfort from it that though God seem long to forget his people's burdens and troubles and cares and prayers, he will at length make it appear that they are not out of his mind. On the name he reports two accounts without choosing: some make its etymology much the same with that of Ishmael, heard of God, because the mother's prayers were remarkably heard; others, taking their cue from the reason she gives, make it asked of God — and it comes nearly to the same, since by either she designed to perpetuate the remembrance of God's favour in answering her, so that at every mention of the name she might take the comfort to herself and give God the glory. Mercies given in answer to prayer, he adds, are to be remembered with peculiar expressions of thankfulness, and how many seasonable deliverances and supplies might we call Samuels, asked of God; whatever is so we are in a special manner engaged to devote to him, and a child of prayer is in a special manner bound to be a good child.
Wesley glosses the verb of remembering by its effect, that God manifested his remembrance of Hannah by what followed.

Ellicott reads the verse as another notice of the pious customs of this household, a striking picture of one of the many holy homes that existed in Israel even in the wild, disorderly days of the Judges, standing against the deep degradation of the priests at the sanctuary; he notes in passing that the house at Ramah uses the short familiar name of the town the first verse called the Ramahs of the Watchers. Keil states the sequence flatly — they worshipped, Elkanah returned home to Ramah with his two wives, he knew his wife Hannah, and Jehovah remembered her, that is, heard her prayer — and is stricter than Henry about the name: it is not formed from the word for name together with the name of God, as one respected lexicon had it, but from a compound meaning heard of God; and the clause because I have asked him of the Lord is not an etymological explanation of the name at all, but an exposition founded upon the facts.

debates.question: What does the name Samuel mean?

positions.position: either heard of God, as Ishmael is, or asked of God from the reason his mother gives; it comes nearly to the same thing
heard of God, from a compound of that sense; the mother's reason is no etymology of the name but an exposition founded on the facts

outliers.note: uses the household's early worship as evidence that many holy homes survived in Israel through the disorder of the Judges, in contrast with the degraded priesthood at the sanctuary

themes: worship before the journey home
the Lord remembered her
what the name Samuel means

20.pericope_label: Samuel born; Hannah stays behind till he is weaned

schools.summary: Gill weighs the phrase that dates the birth, since at the revolutions of days may mean a complete year from their return home, as Ben Melech took it, though he thinks the sense rather the nine months of a woman's going with child. He notes that women might go to the yearly feasts if they pleased but were not obliged to, and leaves open whether Hannah went up at the time appointed for her purification and for the redeeming of a firstborn, since the Scriptures do not relate every fact that was done, though what follows looks rather as if she did not. Of Elkanah's answer he hears a kind and indulgent husband speaking, who knew she would break no law of God by staying and saw that the delay might be better for her health and the child's.

Clarke comes at the name from the reason the mother gives and holds that the Hebrew must be considerably contracted if it is to carry that sense, its components being the words for asked of God — a name to keep both mother and son in continual remembrance of the divine interposition at his birth. He states Hannah's purpose simply, that she would not go up to Shiloh till her son was old enough to be employed in the divine service, and turns the prayer that the Lord would establish his word into a father's petition, that God would preserve the child, cause him to grow up, and make him a blessing to Israel. Wesley draws the inference that though it was nowhere said before, it now appears that the husband had heard his wife's vow and consented to it and had added a vow of his own if God answered their prayers; and he stretches the word weaned further than the others, taking it to mean not only from the breast but from the mother's knee and care and from childish food, until the child was something grown and fit to do some service in the tabernacle — for as soon as he was brought up he worshipped God and presently after was ministering to Eli. The word Elkanah prayed to see established he refers to the vow itself, the matter concerning the child which she had vowed.

Ellicott holds that the words because I have asked him of the Lord do not explain the meaning of the name but simply give the reason for his mother so calling him, the name itself being formed from a compound meaning heard of God. He fixes how long the weaning would take, since it took place very late among the Hebrews and it appears from the books of the Maccabees that mothers were in the habit of suckling their children for three years, after which the mother proposed to leave her son as a servant of the sanctuary all his life. On the prayer that the Lord would establish his word he records the tradition Keil dismisses, in the form Rashi gives it — a voice from heaven went forth saying that there should arise a just one whose name should be Samuel, whereupon every mother who bore a son called him Samuel and, seeing his actions, said this was not he; but when this one was born they said, this is that Samuel — and offers Bunsen's plainer sense for those who decline it, that the Lord would fulfil what he designs with the child and has promised by his birth. Keil points out that the words and his vow show Elkanah to have vowed a vow of his own in case his beloved Hannah should have a son, and that his vow concerned the presentation of a sacrifice, which is why it stands coupled with the yearly offering; and he rejects the Rabbinic view that any direct revelation had been made about Samuel's birth and destination, taking the word to be Eli's — the God of Israel grant thy petition — which the parents might well regard after the birth as a promise from Jehovah himself.

debates.question: What is the word Elkanah asks the Lord to establish?

positions.position: Eli's blessing, which the parents might regard after the birth as a promise from Jehovah himself; no direct revelation was made
on the Rabbinic tradition, a voice from heaven foretelling that a just one named Samuel should arise; failing that, simply what God designs with the child
the vow itself, the matter concerning the child which Hannah had vowed
a father's prayer that God would preserve the child, cause him to grow up, and make him a blessing to Israel

outliers.note: dates the weaning from the customs of the age rather than the text, taking three years from the Maccabean evidence for how long Hebrew mothers suckled their children

themes: Elkanah's own vow
how long the weaning would take
what word Elkanah prayed to see established

24.pericope_label: The child brought to Shiloh and given to the Lord

schools.summary: Gill leaves the number of the beasts open, allowing that the singular in the next verse may stand for the plural or that one alone was slain, and adds that the beast slain may have been a present to Eli at the boy's introduction to him. He hears the mother's opening words through the Targum, which makes them a request rather than an address — I beseech thee, my lord — that Eli would look upon her son, take him under his care as a scholar to be instructed in the law, and enter him into his service; and he supposes Eli might well be backward to it, a Levite not being admitted to service before twenty-five. Of the last words he says she gave the child to be employed in God's service not for a few days or years but for his whole life, as the Targum has it, that he may minister before the Lord: having received him from God as an answer of prayer, she gave him up to God again according to her vow.

Clarke prefers the reading of the Greek, Syriac and Arabic, a bullock of three years old rather than three bullocks, and argues it from the next verse, where they slay the bullock and no more are heard of, a beast of that age being the one ordinarily used; he notes that the bottle was a skin, their vessels for wine being made of goat skins stripped off whole and sewn up. He defends the received rendering of the closing words on grammatical ground: the root means he asked, and in one of its conjugations the verb signifies to lend — a double sense the Vulgate, Septuagint and Syriac all follow, so that lent him to the Lord answers to the asked of him two verses earlier. On the final clause he reports manuscripts and versions reading and they worshipped, and thinks everything from her address to the end of the song is likely Hannah's own, so that it should read and she worshipped there. Wesley keeps the three bullocks and assigns them, one for a burnt-offering, the second for a sin-offering, the third for a peace-offering, taking the singular in the next verse for the plural, which is frequent; the flour he refers to the meal-offerings belonging to the chief sacrifices. He keeps the word lent and turns it into comfort — she lent him, but not with any purpose of requiring him again, and whatever we give to God may in that sense be said to be lent to him, since though we may not recall it he will certainly repay it to our unspeakable advantage — and takes the closing clause of the boy, not Eli, since young Samuel could worship in some sort, at least with outward adoration.

Ellicott stops at the form of the oath, noting that as thy soul liveth is peculiar to these books, occurring six times here and only once in Kings, which accords with the age of the Judges and of Saul being characteristically the age of vows. He calls the rendering I have lent him flatly false and would have it, therefore I also make him one asked of the Lord, all the days that he liveth he is asked of the Lord, the sense being that the Lord gave him to her and she now returns him whom she obtained by prayer; and he takes the last clause of the boy Samuel, putting his own child-seal to his mother's gift of him. Keil keeps the three oxen and explains the singular differently, as pointing to the particular sacrifice that went with the presentation — the burnt-offering by which the boy was consecrated to a lifelong service at the sanctuary — the other two being brought for another use. He describes what her words did, that at the presentation of the boy his mother made herself known to the high priest as the woman who had prayed to the Lord in that very place; and with Ellicott he traces the error in the received rendering, since the meaning to lend which the lexicons give has no support but a false rendering in the Greek, Jehovah having not lent the son to Hannah at all.

debates.question: How many beasts did Hannah bring, and why does the next verse name one?

positions.position: one only; the Greek, Syriac and Arabic read a bullock of three years old, and no more than the one is ever heard of
three, the singular being put for the plural, one for a burnt-offering, one for a sin-offering, one for a peace-offering
three, the one named being the burnt-offering that consecrated the boy, the other two serving another use
the question is open; the one slain may even have been a present to Eli

debates.question: Should the closing words be rendered lent to the Lord?

positions.position: yes; the root that means to ask signifies to lend in one of its conjugations, and the Vulgate, Septuagint and Syriac all follow the double sense
no; the rendering is false and rests on a mistake in the Greek — she makes him one asked of the Lord, returning what she obtained by prayer
the word may stand, since whatever we give to God is lent to him in this sense, that he will certainly repay it
the boy Samuel, putting his own child-seal to his mother's gift of him
Hannah, on the reading of several manuscripts and versions, the whole passage to the end of her song being her words

outliers.note: notes that the oath as thy soul liveth belongs almost entirely to Samuel and Kings, which fits the age of the Judges and Saul being characteristically the age of vows
